question: Can one scalar extracted from a model-based stochastic update explain how convex convergence bounds, and qualitatively nonconvex training loss, degrade as a user-specified base step size grows for SGD, stochastic Polyak steps, non-negative Gauss-Newton steps, and stochastic proximal point updates?

key_findings.claim: The stability index is a one-step, surrogate-dependent quantity that measures the gap between current sampled loss and the regularized model value attained by the next update.
key_findings.evidence: For the model-based proximal update x[t+1]=argmin_y f_x[t](y,s[t])+||y-x[t]||^2/(2 alpha[t]), the paper defines delta[t]=f(x[t],s[t])-f_x[t](x[t+1],s[t])-||x[t+1]-x[t]||^2/(2 alpha[t]). Under model agreement and lower-bound assumptions it is nonnegative. Because delta changes with the chosen surrogate even at the same point and batch, it is a property of an algorithm-model representation, not a unique stability property of the objective alone.

anchors.section: Appendix A.1 / Regularized model proof setup

key_findings.claim: In the convex model setting, expected stability indices enter both average-iterate and last-iterate suboptimality bounds explicitly.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 3.2 telescopes weighted suboptimality into an initial-distance term plus sum alpha[t] E[delta[t]]. Theorem 3.3 divides this term by total step size for a weighted average or best expected iterate; Theorem 3.4 adds harmonic-style weighted history terms for the last iterate. Thus smaller delta at the realized trajectory tightens these bounds, conditional on convex model assumptions A1-A2.

key_findings.claim: The weakly convex extension makes delta enter a Moreau-envelope stationarity bound, but it does not justify arbitrary large steps in the nonconvex regime.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.6 assumes weak model/objective conditions, a smoothing parameter bar-rho greater than rho+lambda, and alpha[t] in (0,1/bar-rho). It bounds a weighted sum of squared Moreau-envelope gradients by envelope decrease plus E[delta]. These restrictions are materially different from the very large alpha experiments and from an unconstrained claim that adaptive updates remain stable for any nonconvex step size.

key_findings.claim: For SGD the index grows linearly in the user step size, while the SPS index is capped and no larger at the same iterate and batch.
key_findings.evidence: The linear model gives delta_SGD=alpha[t]||g[t]||^2/2. The truncated lower-bounded model yields the SPS update with effective step tau[t]=min(alpha[t],(f-C)/||g||^2) and delta_SPS=tau[t](1-tau[t]/(2 alpha[t]))||g[t]||^2, bounded by both the SGD value and min(alpha[t]||g||^2,f-C). Appendix A.2 explicitly states that the inequality assumes both indices are measured at the same x[t] and s[t].

key_findings.claim: SPS's expected advantage depends on interpolation and lower-bound accuracy, and the paper's negative experiments confirm that either can erase it.
key_findings.evidence: The expected cap decomposes into current suboptimality, interpolation constant sigma^2=f(x*)-E inf_z f(z,s), and lower-bound estimation error epsilon_lb=E[inf_z f(z,s)-C_s]. In noisy regression SPS worsens; raising batch size helps SPP but not SPS with C=0; setting C=-2 in the noiseless case removes SPS's advantage. On vowel logistic regression, the paper reports almost no SPS advantage, attributing it to lower-bound error.

anchors.section: 5.2 / Variants V1-V3 and vowel null result

key_findings.claim: NGN has a saturating local index, but the convergence framework only partially covers it because model lower-bound assumptions need additional regularity.
key_findings.evidence: For nonnegative loss, the square-root-linearize-square model produces effective step gamma[t]=alpha[t]/(1+alpha[t]||g[t]||^2/(2f[t])) and delta_NGN=gamma[t]||g[t]||^2/2 <= delta_SGD; gamma saturates as alpha grows. However, satisfying the second weak-model assumption requires an inequality related to exp-concavity or a bounded domain in the convex case. The contributions accordingly say the theory applies only 'partially NGN,' so the exact index inequality is broader than the available global convergence theorem.

key_findings.claim: SPP receives a sublinear/capped index bound under convexity, but exact proximal subproblems and weak-convex step restrictions limit practical and theoretical scope.
key_findings.evidence: For convex sampled loss, delta_SPP is bounded by min(alpha[t]||g[t]||^2/2, f(x[t],s[t])-inf_y f(y,s[t])) and its expectation by suboptimality plus sigma^2. For eta-weakly convex sampled losses the denominator 1-alpha[t] eta requires alpha[t]<1/eta. The paper notes that exact SPP is generally a theoretical method unless special structure makes the subproblem competitive; no deep-network SPP experiment is run.

anchors.section: Appendix A.2-A.3 / SPP proof and quadratic special case

key_findings.claim: The headline that SPS or NGN is 'always more stable' is a same-state local comparison, not an unconditional dominance result for their distinct optimization trajectories or final losses.
key_findings.evidence: The proof compares delta_method and delta_SGD at an identical x[t], stochastic batch s[t], gradient, and base alpha. Once algorithms run, they visit different states and see different gradients and losses, so pointwise delta ordering need not order the sums in their respective convergence bounds or their final objectives. The experiments generally support the expected pattern but include regimes with no advantage; the paper itself says its goal is qualitative explanation rather than proving superior practical performance.

anchors.section: Abstract and contributions / Always less sensitive claim

key_findings.claim: The PEP calculation supports tightness of the one-step SPP upper bound in a constrained convex class, not whole-run optimizer optimality.
key_findings.evidence: The Performance Estimation Problem fixes one point, one sampled convex lower-bounded function, an objective gap at most one, and gradient norm at most G. Numerically, the worst-case delta nearly reaches min(alpha G^2/2, f(x)-inf f), except near the transition. This validates a local bound shape under those constraints; it does not compare stochastic trajectories, wall-clock proximal cost, or nonconvex training.

key_findings.claim: The generic convergence-rate conversion is a negative result: it discards the adaptive stability benefit and recovers only the ordinary convex Lipschitz SGD rate.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B.1 upper-bounds SPS and NGN delta by delta_SGD, then with constant alpha and bounded gradients obtains O(1/sqrt(T)), exactly the standard SGD rate. The conclusion says this conversion is too coarse to show a speedup. Thus the theory quantifies learning-rate sensitivity in a trajectory-dependent bound but does not establish faster worst-case convergence for the adaptive methods.

key_findings.claim: On ResNet20/CIFAR10, SPS and NGN tolerate roughly an order of magnitude larger base rates than constant-rate SGD in a short 20-epoch run.
key_findings.evidence: Across alpha from 10^-2 to 10^2, constant-rate SGD begins degrading at alpha>=1 while SPS and NGN work to approximately 10. The logged stability indices grow much more slowly for SPS/NGN early in training, and the convex last-iterate bound qualitatively selects a similar good-rate region. Three runs share the same initialization and differ only in data ordering.

key_findings.claim: The ResNet bound match is post hoc and outside the convex theorem's assumptions, so it is qualitative diagnostic evidence rather than validation of the theorem on deep learning.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.4 assumes convex models A1-A2, while ResNet training is explicitly nonconvex. Its unknown distance D is set to 50 after observing ||x_T-x_1|| approximately 50, and the footnote calls this highly approximate because method/rate pairs with similar loss can have distinct model norms. Appendix sweeps D from 1 to 100 and the horizon from 20 to 10 epochs, preserving the qualitative curve, but does not turn the bound into a prospective computable certificate.

anchors.section: Appendix E / D and horizon ablations

key_findings.claim: A short linear warmup is a meaningful negative control for the simple SGD-versus-adaptive narrative.
key_findings.evidence: Warming SGD from 10^-10 to the base rate over 100 iterations lets it work reasonably for about one order of magnitude larger alpha and suppresses the initial delta explosion. The bound reflects this improvement. Because SPS/NGN are compared mainly to constant-rate SGD and schedules are not equally optimized, part of the apparent algorithmic stability gap can be recovered by a standard schedule intervention.

key_findings.claim: In interpolating synthetic linear regression, SPS and SPP remain effective across much larger base steps than SGD, matching the index caps.
key_findings.evidence: With n=50, d=10, batch 5, and exactly fit targets, SPS and SPP retain reasonable training loss to alpha=100 while SGD starts failing around 0.03. The last-iterate bound with D=1 mirrors the range and SPP overtakes SPS for alpha>=1. The result is a clean convex demonstration but uses a tiny synthetic, deliberately interpolating problem.

anchors.section: Appendix A / Exact ridge-SPP linear system

key_findings.claim: The regression variants expose method-specific failure modes rather than universal robustness.
key_findings.evidence: Adding target noise makes SPS and SPP worse because interpolation is lost while mini-batches remain individually fit; increasing batch size to 25 reduces SPP's interpolation constant and restores its relative advantage, but SPS with lower bound C=0 does not gain; in noiseless data, an intentionally loose C=-2 causes SPS to lose all advantage. These results agree with the proposed decomposition and directly qualify 'always stable' language.

anchors.section: Appendix B.2 / Large-alpha and bad-lower-bound regimes

key_findings.claim: The real convex classification experiment includes a null outcome: SPS offers almost no benefit on vowel when its lower bound is poorly specified.
key_findings.evidence: For LIBSVM vowel, the authors state that SPS shows almost no advantage over SGD, likely from lower-bound estimation error, while NGN is less affected. Appendix specifies only 416 retained vowel examples, 10 dimensions, 11 classes, batch 16, and 20 epochs; DNA has 1,600 examples, 180 dimensions, three classes, batch 16, and 10 epochs. Extra plots show validation/DNA trends but no statistical intervals.

key_findings.claim: The empirical section tests stability as final training loss over base rates, not bounded iterates, generalization, numerical safety, or competitive end-task performance.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5 explicitly prioritizes training loss and says its goal is not to establish superior SPS/NGN performance. The ResNet run is 20 epochs, convex regressions are small, SPP is omitted from deep learning, and validation loss appears only as an appendix similarity check. No Adam, momentum, weight decay, tuned cosine schedule, wall-clock proximal cost, or modern optimizer comparison is included.

key_findings.claim: Appendix D contains a secondary novel log-exp/Lambert-W adaptive step, but only a preliminary stability observation, not a validated contribution.
key_findings.evidence: Generalizing square-root-linearize-square to invertible convex map pairs preserves delta<=delta_SGD. Choosing log then exp yields gamma=(f/||g||^2) W_0(alpha||g||^2/f). The authors say this step appears novel and is stable in preliminary experiments, but provide no plot, benchmark, convergence theorem specialized to it, or comparison because it lies outside the paper's focus.

key_findings.claim: The paper's practical reach is deliberately limited: it produces no step-selection or early-termination rule and excludes the optimizer components most commonly used in modern training.
key_findings.evidence: The authors leave open how to exploit tracked delta, including whether to terminate unstable runs. Their model-based analysis excludes momentum, weight decay, and preconditioning/Adam, even though related SPS variants can incorporate them. The result is explanatory theory for a selected family, not a deployable learning-rate controller or general theory of optimizer robustness.

anchors.section: 6 / Practical open questions and excluded geometries

method.core_idea: Expose learning-rate sensitivity through the regularized surrogate value of a single model-based update, then propagate that one-step quantity into convex or weakly convex bounds and compare its scaling across optimizer models.
method.mechanism: Write SGD, SPS, NGN, and SPP as stochastic model-based proximal updates. Define delta as current sampled loss minus the selected surrogate-plus-proximal objective value. Under convex lower-model assumptions, telescope distances to a solution to obtain average- and last-iterate bounds containing weighted expected delta. Under weak convexity, insert delta into a Moreau-envelope stationarity bound with restricted steps. Derive exact or upper-bound delta formulas for the linear, truncated, square-root, and exact models, then log gradient norms and batch losses along training runs to calculate the formulas and compare the resulting bound curves with final loss over a base-rate sweep.
assumptions: The stochastic objective admits a solution and sampled losses have suitable subgradients.
For convex suboptimality results, every surrogate is convex, agrees with the sampled loss at the current point, and globally lower-bounds that sampled loss.
For weakly convex results, model and sampled-loss weak-convexity constants exist, expected approximation error is finite, and every alpha[t] is below the stated inverse curvature bound.
The same proximal regularization coefficient places the user base-rate alpha on a comparable scale across distinct surrogate models.
SPS has a valid per-sample lower bound C_s; its practical benefit depends on interpolation sigma^2 and lower-bound error epsilon_lb.
NGN losses are nonnegative, and the additional surrogate lower-model condition needed for the global theorem holds on the relevant domain.
SPP subproblems are solved exactly and are computationally accessible in the problem structure considered.
Expected one-step delta values along realized trajectories can be estimated adequately by a few data-ordering runs.
A distance D from initialization to a comparator is known or can be meaningfully approximated when plotting the bound.
Qualitative similarity between a convex bound and nonconvex ResNet loss is informative even though the theorem assumptions fail.
Final training loss after a short horizon is an adequate operational measure of step-size stability.
Holding the current iterate and batch fixed is the relevant counterfactual for pointwise optimizer-index comparisons.

techniques.role: Represents four stochastic optimizers as the minimization of a local surrogate plus a common quadratic regularizer.
Measures how much regularized surrogate value the next step removes from the current sampled loss.
Turns one-step model improvement into weighted average- and last-iterate convex suboptimality bounds.
Uses envelope gradients as a stationarity measure for weakly convex objectives.
Caps an SGD-like step using the gap to a sampled-loss lower bound.
Uses loss nonnegativity to derive a saturating Gauss-Newton effective step.
Bounds sensitivity through the exact proximal improvement and interpolation gap.
Numerically tests worst-case tightness of the one-step SPP index bound over convex lower-bounded functions.
Computes method-specific delta from batch loss and gradient norm at every experimental step.
Separates a user scale alpha from a schedule eta[t] and tests several orders of magnitude.
Explains when SPS/SPP caps remain useful through sigma-squared and lower-bound estimation error.
Generalizes NGN by transforming, linearizing, and inverse-transforming a nonnegative loss.

evaluations.metric: Average- and last-iterate expected suboptimality upper bounds
evaluations.result: Both bounds contain weighted E[delta[t]]; their large-alpha behavior is benign only when delta grows sublinearly or is capped
evaluations.baseline: Standard distance telescoping with the SGD variance term alpha||g||^2/2

evaluations.setting: Fixed iterate, batch, gradient, and base step for SGD versus SPS/NGN/SPP
evaluations.result: SPS and NGN indices are no greater than SGD; convex SPP has the same upper-bound ordering; all three flatten as alpha grows

evaluations.setting: PEPit convex worst-case calculation for SPP
evaluations.metric: Maximum one-step delta under unit objective gap and gradient bound G
evaluations.result: The computed worst case nearly saturates min(alpha G^2/2, f(x)-inf f), except near the transition

evaluations.setting: ResNet20 on CIFAR10 for 20 epochs, alpha in [10^-2,10^2], three identical-initialization/data-order runs
evaluations.metric: Final train loss and convex last-iterate bound curve
evaluations.result: Constant-rate SGD degrades at alpha>=1; SPS and NGN work to about alpha=10; the post-hoc-D bound mirrors the good-rate range
evaluations.baseline: SGD with constant schedule and SGD with 100-step linear warmup

evaluations.metric: Range of usable alpha and early delta growth
evaluations.result: A 100-iteration warmup expands SGD's useful range by roughly one order of magnitude and suppresses early index explosion

evaluations.setting: Interpolating linear regression, n=50, d=10, batch 5
evaluations.metric: Final training loss over alpha and last-iterate bound
evaluations.result: SPS/SPP remain reasonable through alpha=100, SGD fails around 0.03, and SPP overtakes SPS at alpha>=1

evaluations.setting: Noisy regression and lower-bound/batch variants V1-V3
evaluations.result: Noise worsens SPS/SPP; batch 25 restores SPP but not SPS; C=-2 removes SPS advantage even without noise
evaluations.baseline: Noiseless interpolating regression with C=0 and batch 5

evaluations.setting: LIBSVM vowel multiclass logistic regression, 416 samples, d=10, batch 16, 20 epochs
evaluations.metric: Final train loss and bound over alpha
evaluations.result: SPS has almost no advantage over SGD under lower-bound error; NGN is less affected
evaluations.baseline: SGD, SPS, and NGN under the same base-rate sweep

evaluations.setting: Generic convex Lipschitz rate conversion for SPS and NGN
evaluations.result: Using delta<=delta_SGD yields O(1/sqrt(T)), the same order as SGD and no adaptive speedup

evaluations.setting: Log-exp/Lambert-W adaptive step in Appendix D
evaluations.metric: Analytic one-step index inequality and unspecified preliminary experiments
evaluations.result: Derived delta<=delta_SGD and claimed preliminary stability, but no reported quantitative benchmark or specialized convergence result

limitations: Author-stated: large parts of the framework require convexity and cover only a selected model-based family.
Author-stated: the analysis excludes momentum, weight decay, preconditioning, Adam, and other update geometries prevalent in practice.
Author-stated: the paper does not turn delta tracking into a practical rate selector, scheduler, or early-termination heuristic.
Author-stated: the current generic conversion to a convergence rate is too coarse to show an SPS/NGN speedup.
Author-stated: exact SPP proximal subproblems can be impractical outside special statistical-learning structures.
Reviewer-identified: 'always more stable' is proved pointwise at the same iterate and batch, not along distinct algorithm trajectories.
Reviewer-identified: the ResNet comparison applies a convex theorem outside its assumptions and selects D from the observed trajectory.
Reviewer-identified: three runs use identical initialization and vary only data order; no uncertainty bars or significance analysis are reported.
Reviewer-identified: final training loss operationalizes stability but does not measure bounded iterates, generalization, calibration, or numerical faults.
Reviewer-identified: the 20-epoch ResNet horizon emphasizes early instability and does not establish long-horizon optimizer quality.
Reviewer-identified: schedules and optimizer components are not comparably tuned; warmup alone substantially narrows the apparent gap.
Reviewer-identified: no deep-network SPP result tests its theoretical cap against computational cost.
Reviewer-identified: NGN's pointwise formula requires only nonnegative loss, but its global convex framework needs an extra model-lower-bound condition.
Reviewer-identified: the synthetic and LIBSVM convex tasks are small, and the vowel advantage is null for SPS.
Reviewer-identified: the Appendix D step is declared novel after preliminary experiments but lacks a literature-wide novelty search, full theorem, or evaluation within the paper.
failure_modes: A poor sampled-loss lower bound makes epsilon_lb large and can eliminate SPS's cap advantage despite a large nominal alpha range.
Non-interpolating noise leaves per-batch minima below the population optimum, inflating sigma-squared and degrading SPS/SPP.
Changing batch size changes the sampled infimum and therefore SPP's stability constant; optimizer rankings need not be batch-invariant.
A same-state index advantage can disappear after methods follow different trajectories with different gradients and sampled losses.
Weak convexity imposes alpha below an inverse-curvature limit; arbitrary large-step conclusions can fail outside convexity.
NGN may lack the model lower-bound/exp-concavity condition needed to place its index inside the advertised convergence theorem.
Exact SPP can be computationally slower than SGD even when its iteration-level bound is less sensitive.
A post-hoc D can make a theoretical curve appear descriptive without enabling prospective step-size selection.
Warmup or another schedule can recover much of constant-SGD's apparent instability, making a base-rate-only comparison schedule-dependent.
The index can be small while convergence remains slow because the bias term scales inversely with accumulated step size.
Modern momentum/preconditioned updates fall outside the Euclidean model-based comparison and may reverse qualitative rankings.
reusable_insights: Separate large-step sensitivity from best-tuned convergence rate: an optimizer can have the same optimal rate yet a much wider usable hyperparameter range.
Express optimizer updates through a common regularized surrogate before comparing their user-facing step scales.
Audit every pointwise optimizer inequality for whether it holds at the same state or along each method's realized trajectory.
Decompose adaptive-step behavior into interpolation error and lower-bound error; both suggest concrete batch/noise stress tests.
Track one-step quantities during training, but distinguish retrospective explanatory bounds from prospectively computable certificates.
Include warmup and schedule controls whenever claiming an optimizer intrinsically tolerates a wider learning-rate range.
Use negative regimes with noise, larger batches, and deliberately wrong lower bounds to validate what a theory says should erase an advantage.
Moreau-envelope stationarity provides a principled weakly convex target, but all inverse-curvature step restrictions must remain visible.
Invertible transform-linearize-inverse-transform constructions can generate adaptive steps whose sensitivity caps follow from convexity of the inverse map.
Evaluate iteration bounds jointly with subproblem wall time when comparing proximal and first-order methods.
open_questions: Can trajectory-specific SPS/NGN index caps be converted into a rate that is strictly better than the generic O(1/sqrt(T)) bound?
What conditions turn same-iterate delta ordering into ordering of cumulative delta along different algorithm trajectories?
Can D and the expected delta terms be upper-bounded online to make the plotted bound a prospective learning-rate controller?
Does the qualitative bound match persist for long-horizon large-model training under cosine decay, weight decay, clipping, and momentum?
How should the stability index be defined for Adam, Muon, natural-gradient, and other preconditioned geometries?
Can SPP's proximal subproblem cost be included in a stability-versus-wall-clock theorem and deep-network experiment?
Which practical lower-bound estimators keep SPS error controlled under non-interpolation and label noise?
How many seeds and which initialization variations are needed to distinguish stable-rate range changes reliably?
Does a low index predict validation/generalization stability, or only training-loss tolerance to large alpha?
Can the log-exp/Lambert-W step be given complete convex/nonconvex rates and competitive benchmarks?
Is there a model-invariant index, or do alternative valid surrogates give meaningfully different stability diagnoses for the same update?

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic (Approximate) Proximal Point Methods: Convergence, Optimality, and Adaptivity
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational direct predecessor for the aProx/model-based update family, convex lower-model assumptions, and robustness of richer stochastic models.
competitive_landscape.difference: Asi and Duchi establish almost-sure stability, convergence, asymptotic optimality, adaptivity, and experiments for approximate proximal models. The reviewed paper reuses that framework but introduces a non-asymptotic one-step index aimed specifically at scaling with a user step size and at cross-method SGD/SPS/NGN/SPP comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic model-based minimization of weakly convex functions
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational primary predecessor for weakly convex stochastic models, Moreau-envelope stationarity, and complexity guarantees.
competitive_landscape.difference: Davis and Drusvyatskiy prove rates for stochastic proximal point, proximal subgradient, and regularized Gauss-Newton models under approximation/regularity conditions. The reviewed paper's weak-convex contribution is to expose E[delta] inside a related envelope bound and compare its alpha scaling, not to originate the model-based weak-convex framework.

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic Polyak Step-size for SGD: An Adaptive Learning Rate for Fast Convergence
competitive_landscape.relationship: Primary source for capped SPS, its interpolation-dependent convergence theory, and the empirical claim that it reduces learning-rate tuning.
competitive_landscape.difference: Loizou et al. analyze convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex SPS and emphasize fast convergence in interpolation. The reviewed paper derives an exact local index, separates interpolation from lower-bound error, and argues that the earlier bound grows linearly in alpha where empirical SPS remains stable; its own generic rate still falls back to O(1/sqrt(T)).

competitive_landscape.title: An Adaptive Stochastic Gradient Method with Non-negative Gauss-Newton Stepsizes
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct primary source for NGN's square-root Gauss-Newton update, nonnegativity mechanism, convergence theory, and empirical stability.
competitive_landscape.difference: Orvieto and Xiao introduce NGN and give smooth convex/nonconvex analyses showing automatic warmup/decay. The reviewed paper does not introduce NGN; it re-expresses it as a model, derives delta_NGN<=delta_SGD, and extends a pessimistic complexity to convex nonsmooth loss while acknowledging only partial compatibility with its lower-model assumptions.

competitive_landscape.title: Cutting Some Slack for SGD with Adaptive Polyak Stepsizes
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct practical SPS competitor that explicitly targets non-interpolation and unknown/poor lower bounds through a learned slack variable.
competitive_landscape.difference: Gower et al. propose and evaluate nonlinear slack-SPS variants with convergence theory. The reviewed paper instead diagnoses ordinary capped SPS through epsilon_lb and sigma-squared, and demonstrates bad-bound failure; it does not compare its diagnostic or experiments against the slack variants designed for that failure mode.

competitive_landscape.title: Revisiting Stochastic Proximal Point Methods: Generalized Smoothness and Similarity
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest current SPP theory competitor, explicitly motivated by SPP's step-size stability and low tuning burden.
competitive_landscape.difference: Tovmasyan et al. give full SPP convergence analyses under phi-smoothness and expected similarity, including regimes beyond traditional smoothness. The reviewed paper focuses on a one-step cap that makes SPP comparable to SGD/SPS/NGN and notes those stronger SPP rates require extra assumptions; it adds cross-method sensitivity interpretation rather than a more comprehensive SPP rate.

competitive_landscape.title: New Perspectives on the Polyak Stepsize: Surrogate Functions and Negative Results
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest negative-results competitor for Polyak steps, proving that nonconvergence suggested by some bounds is real under misspecification and large steps.
competitive_landscape.difference: Orabona and D'Orazio unify Polyak variants through surrogate losses and construct genuine failure cases. The reviewed paper cites and reconciles those cases via simultaneous growth of lower-bound error and alpha; this prevents its same-point SPS index inequality from being read as unconditional convergence or trajectory stability under arbitrary lower-bound estimates.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper identifies a stability index that directly determines large-step sensitivity in model-based stochastic optimization, proves SPS and NGN are always at least as stable as SGD and SPP has a favorable cap, provides the first convex nonsmooth NGN complexity, and shows the resulting bound mirrors performance even for nonconvex deep learning.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Delta enters new average/last-iterate convex and weak-convex stationarity bounds; closed forms or caps are derived for four models; PEP nearly saturates the SPP cap; ResNet, synthetic regression, and LIBSVM sweeps qualitatively align with the bound; Appendix B derives an NGN O(1/sqrt(T)) nonsmooth rate.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest defensible novelty is a clear, comparable one-step sensitivity decomposition and its insertion into non-asymptotic model-based bounds, plus well-chosen negative experiments that expose interpolation and lower-bound-error regimes. The optimizer models, aProx/weak-convex framework, SPS, NGN, and SPP stability are prior work. 'Always more stable' must retain the same-iterate-and-batch qualifier, and the current rate shows no speedup. The nonconvex ResNet result is a useful empirical analogy based on a post-hoc distance, not an extension of the convex theorem. Appendix D's Lambert-W step may be novel but is insufficiently evaluated to count as a mature primary contribution.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text review of the current official target revision arXiv:2602.09842v2 (2026-05-26). I reviewed all 19 physical PDF pages: main theory and experiments, both reference pages, Appendix A's complete proofs and quadratic special case, Appendix B's rate comparison and negative-result reconciliation, Appendix C's data generation and exact dataset table, Appendix D's full generalized-map and Lambert-W derivation, and every supplemental plot through page 19. Page anchors use physical PDF numbering and were checked against the indexed extraction with no missing pages. Every finding has an attribution, with explicit contradiction audits for same-state versus trajectory claims, convex versus nonconvex scope, post-hoc D, warmup, and rate-versus-stability language, plus the reported null/negative regimes. Seven direct primary competitors were researched on official arXiv records, checked 2026-08-23, and pinned to exact current revisions. Confidence is high for formula, theorem-scope, table, and appendix fidelity, but not 1 because proofs were read rather than independently rederived in full and the experiments/code were not reproduced.
